title: US Law Firms Probe HDFC Bank Over Alleged Maharashtra Deposit Payments
excerpt: Three separate US securities firms are investigating whether India's largest private lender misled investors about ₹45 crore in payments disguised as marketing expenses.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Three US law firms are investigating HDFC Bank for potential securities law violations.
  • Allegations involve ₹45 crore disguised as marketing expenses to secure deposits.
  • HDFC Bank's ADRs fell 4% following the allegations, indicating shareholder harm.
  • The bank denies wrongdoing, claiming the issue is not material to its finances.
  • Increased scrutiny follows former chairman's resignation over governance concerns.

Three US law firms have launched independent investigations into HDFC Bank, examining whether India's largest private-sector lender violated federal securities laws by allegedly disguising payments to a state agency to attract deposits.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=xjwOBDneI1M

Los Angeles-based Glancy Prongay & Rotter LLP, the Law Offices of Howard G. Smith in Bensalem, Pennsylvania, and the Law Offices of Frank R. Cruz in Century City, California, each announced they are probing the bank and inviting shareholders who suffered losses to come forward. Glancy's announcement was published on Business Wire on July 22.

The ₹45 Crore Allegations

The investigations trace back to a report by The Indian Express published on May 27 alleging that HDFC Bank conducted an internal vigilance probe into payments routed through its marketing department. According to the report, the bank allegedly disguised approximately ₹45 crore ($5.3 million) as sponsorship expenses for road safety campaigns. The payments were allegedly meant to compensate the Maharashtra State Road Development Corporation (MSRDC) through differential interest to secure large deposits from the state agency.

The report further alleged the arrangement may have violated Reserve Bank of India regulations, which prohibit banks from offering negotiated interest rates to individual depositors.

Investors reacted swiftly. HDFC Bank's NYSE-listed American Depositary Receipts, which trade under the ticker HDB, fell $1.02 — approximately 4.1% — to close at $23.78 on May 27, according to The Economic Times. The law firms cite this decline as evidence that the disclosure caused direct financial harm to shareholders.

"The bank has robust internal oversight, audit and control processes and systems. All issues are dealt with in accordance with the bank's established norms, and full process is always followed before final determination post any internal review. We strongly reject any assumptions of wrongdoing or culpability based on selective material."

— HDFC Bank, statement issued May 27

Bank Tells SEC Matter Is Not Material

The day after the allegations surfaced, HDFC Bank filed a Form 6-K with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on May 28, furnishing a clarificatory response it had sent to Indian stock exchanges. The filing, signed by Company Secretary Ajay Agarwal, stated that the bank's internal audit function routinely conducts reviews and that observations in the matter were being "comprehensively addressed."

The bank emphasized the issue does not have a material impact on its financial statements and that no disclosure obligation under SEBI's Regulation 30 had been triggered — signaling it considers the reported matter non-material.

Broader Governance Spotlight

The US probes arrive against a backdrop of heightened governance scrutiny at India's most valuable private bank. Former Chairman Atanu Chakraborty resigned in March, citing "certain happenings and practices within the bank" that conflicted with his personal values. He later indicated that alleged mis-selling of Credit Suisse perpetual bonds was one issue behind his differences with management. An independent review by Wilson Sonsini Goodrich & Rosati and Wadia Ghandy & Co. found no evidence to support Chakraborty's allegations, according to Mint.

What US-Based Investors Should Watch

None of the three firms has disclosed whether their investigations have progressed to a formal class-action filing. In typical US securities litigation, early-stage investigation announcements serve to identify a lead plaintiff before petitioning a federal court — a process that can take weeks to months.

Glancy has set up a dedicated case page for HDB investors and flagged the matter under the SEC's whistleblower programme, noting that individuals with non-public information could be eligible for an award of up to 30% of any amount the SEC recovers. Howard G. Smith and Frank R. Cruz have similarly opened case files soliciting affected shareholders.

With a market capitalization of approximately $125 billion, HDFC Bank remains one of the most widely held Indian stocks among diaspora investors. Any escalation to a formal class action could test investor confidence in the lender's governance disclosures at a time when the bank is already navigating post-merger integration challenges.
